#742. Germany news: Merz hopes for Korean reunification at DMZ

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed hope for Korean reunification during a visit to the heavily fortified border. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier has held talks with China's Xi Jinping in Beijing.

Below, you can review the leading headlines from and about Germany from Friday, October 30:

Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea

Merz draws on Germany's own reunification experience, saying division causes suffering

Two German leaders, two parallel missions across Asia.

While President Frank-Walter Steinmeier sought to reinforce ties with China in Beijing, Chancellor Friedrich Merz toured Japan, South Korea and Singapore, promoting closer cooperation among what he calls the world's "middle powers."

Together, the visits highlight Berlin's effort to lower risks without decoupling from China.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's annual inflation rate eased to 2.8% in October from 3.3% in September, with economists pointing to the government's fuel tax cut as the main reason.

Preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office showed energy prices rose 12.2% compared with a year earlier, down from 14.9% in September. Services inflation slowed to 2.5%, while food inflation remained at 0.4%.

"The decisive factor was the fuel tax cut," said Silke Tober of the Macroeconomic Policy Institute. The reduction took effect in October and runs through December, although rising crude oil prices partly offset the savings at the pump.

ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski said higher energy costs had yet to feed through into broader price increases. Unlike during the 2022 energy crisis, consumers were unwilling or unable to absorb substantially higher prices, he said.

But economists warned the relief could prove temporary. "Gas and oil prices have risen significantly again in recent weeks," said Stephanie Schoenwald, an economist at Germany's state-owned development bank KfW, citing continuing conflicts and lower inventories.

German President's Frank-Walter Steinmeier latest trip to Asia was intended to provide more clarity. Amid a delicate period, Steinmeier sought a balancing act in China between respect and criticism.

It was a state visit of a kind rarely seen today. For four days, Steinmeier traveled across the country: from Hefei, where the German automaker Volkswagen's China operations are headquartered, through historic villages and the imposing landscapes of the Yellow Mountains. He also visited several points of interest of Chinese history, art, and science, and finally, he headed to Tiananmen Square in the heart of Beijing's political center.

Steinmeier—who is set to leave office in March 2027— spoke as a statesman and diplomat on matters of German and European interest. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Steinmeier have known each other for many years, so in this respect, the president was the right man to address even the most difficult issues as a European.

This political balancing act between respect and criticism did not trigger any visible outrage in Beijing.

When he spoke with Chinese leaders about their subsidies for exports to Europe and the related issue of the trade deficit, Xi replied: "I am ready to work together to open a new chapter in the comprehensive strategic partnership between our two countries and to advance the development of global governance."

Just how much willingness lies behind the push for a strategic partnership will become clear during further negotiations between the EU and China.

Xi Jinping seems to understand that a persistent trade deficit with Europe could also become a problem for his country, as an economic crisis in Europe could further strain China's economy.

As "the world's second- and third-largest economies," China and Germany also bear "an important responsibility for the development of relations between China and Europe, as well as for stable growth in the global economy," Xi Jinping said. While that may not sound like a breakthrough yet, it certainly sounds like an understanding.

In contrast to his economic arguments, Steinmeier's political appeals for Beijing to assume more responsibility for the international order fell on deaf ears.

The German president addressed global conflicts and wars on several occasions in Beijing, including Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine. But he received no responses in official statements.

That same evening, the news channel of the Chinese TV network CCTV aired a report that merely covered Steinmeier's visit to a well-known astrophysics institute.

There was no mention of the call for China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, to do more to promote world peace.

Mitat Özdemir is one of more than 870,000 Turkish workers who were recruited to Germany by a government program between 1961 and 1973. He dealt with tough factory work, language barriers and cultural differences.

Six decades later, he and his family still live in Germany. How did the program from back then shape their lives and modern Germany?

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.

North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.

"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.

"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.

North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state."

A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.

The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.

The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.

The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.

Munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories."

The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.

The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.

German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Profits of German luxury car brand Audi for the third quarter came plunged 87% year-on-year to €95 million ($106 million), the Volkswagen subsidiary reported on Friday. This is a drop from €718 million seen in the same quarter last year.

The drop comes amid weak demand in China, and US tariffs.

"Market and competitive conditions have become significantly more difficult in the third quarter," Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger told journalists on a call.

"That all shows that we need to intensify measures and set clear priorities," he added.

Overall in the first nine months of 2026, Audi's profits have dropped 41% to €1.22 billion.

The carmaker trimmed its 2026 profit outlook down to 3 to 5% for the year, down from the previous 5 to 7%.

Audi's sluggish numbers represent more bad news for the 10-brand Volkswagen Group, which on Thursday reported its largest quarterly loss in more than a ‌decade, at nearly €6 billion.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A ban on new Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.

Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.

Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.

"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.

The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.

The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.

"We both bear responsibility for the ⁠international order ​and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.

President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.

"This new paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi said during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.

Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.

The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.

Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.

While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.

In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.

Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.

At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."

Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.

Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.

Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."

Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.

"There is a fear that we might be facing ‌a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ‌ourselves off from other nations," ‌Merz said.

"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, ‌but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference  "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing.

Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Read DW's full report on who may be the next German president.

Good morning from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

Germany's chancellor and president were both in Asia this week, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for more robust trade ties with middle powers and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier focusing on diplomacy   during a multi-day visit to China.

On Friday, Merz spoke at a German-South Korean business conference in Seoul, while Steinmeier is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

#741. Lil Baby Brings ‘Fresh’ to Life: Stream It Now

"Fresh" is the followup to 2025's "WHAM," which arrived at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, one of his four leaders on the all-genres albums chart.

Two weeks after his big reveal, Lil Baby goes and drops Fresh, the followup to WHAM which arrived at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 following its release in February 2025.

The Atlanta native packs it in with 17 Fresh tracks. Just two of those feature guest appearances: “All My Partnas” with Future, Young Thug and 4PF running mate Rylo Rodriguez, plus “In Your Head,” on which Rodriguez gives an assist. Explore Lil Baby See latest videos, charts and news

Sadly, there’s no Sabrina Carpenter collaboration — something the rapper recently admitted he was open to. “I’m still in that box a little bit, but I’m more open to stepping out of the box,” he told The New York Times’ Popcast last month. “The box is bigger. As I step out a little bit, the box gets bigger.” Related Queens of the Stone Age Crowned on ARIA Chart With 'Perfecth' Lil Baby, JENNIE, Dove Cameron, XG, Boys Noize & More: New Music Friday Guide JENNIE's 'Steps' Soundtrack 'Someone to Hold' Is Here: Stream It Now

He added: “Even a Sabrina Carpenter — just say, for instance, in my head, I don’t have a song on my hard drive to send to her. But if we sit there and create something, or she sends me something, I feel like I could make it work.”

The hip-hop star got the wheels moving on his new project in July with “Dead Fresh,” a Pharrell-produced number that cracked the Billboard Hot 100’s top 20, peaking at No. 18. Pharrell premiered “Dead Fresh” during Louis Vuitton’s Spring-Summer 2027 Men’s Show the previous month, in June.

Lil Baby has amassed a ridiculous 160 titles on the Billboard Hot 100, including 13 top 10 appearances, and a further nine titles on the Billboard 200 chart, with four No. 1s. Baby closed out the year 2025 with The Leaks, a mixtape that debuted and peaked at No. 17 on the all-genres albums tally. The Leaks proved to be a late bloomer, as it lifted 25-1 in its second week on Billboard’s Top Rap Albums chart, for his fifth consecutive leader.

Fresh is Baby’s fifth studio album. “S/o To Everyone Who Played A Role In Bringing This Album To Life,” he writes on his Instagram.

#740. Palmer misses too many chances to impress - Tuchel

Thomas Tuchel has named three uncapped players in his England squad

England manager Thomas Tuchel said Cole Palmer "misses too many chances to impress" after not selecting the Chelsea forward for November's Nations League fixtures.

Palmer, 24, dropped out of England's squad for their previous games in early autumn and is absent again for matches against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November and Spain in Madrid on Sunday, 15 November.

Tuchel has instead handed Fulham's Josh King and Borussia Dortmund's Jobe Bellingham their first England call-ups. Both players are attacking midfielders.

"We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together," said Tuchel.

"We have Josh King as a new player in there, but I want to see him on both wings. He is kind of an extra player and he can play all four positions.

"I guess everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception.

"We are speaking now about a player that is not in camp. It counts when you are in camp and I just said last time that he misses too many opportunities to impress."

Jobe, 21, joins his brother Jude in the England squad - and they could be the first pair of siblings to feature in an England line-up since Gary and Phil Neville.

England sit second behind Spain in group A3 of the Nations League with three wins and a loss.

One more point from their remaining two matches will secure a place in the two-legged quarter-finals in March, with the winners of those ties advancing to the Nations League Finals in June.

Catch-up with all Thomas Tuchel's responses at his squad selection news conference

Goalkeepers: Jordan Pickford (Everton), Jason Steele (Brighton & Hove Albion), James Trafford (Leeds United)

Defenders: Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guehi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle United), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen), Djed Spence (Inter Milan), Ben White (Arsenal)

Midfielders: Elliot Anderson (Manchester City), Jobe Bellingham (Borussia Dortmund), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid), James Garner (Everton), Josh King (Fulham), Myles Lewis-Skelly (Arsenal), Declan Rice (Arsenal)

Forwards: Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United), Eberechi Eze (Arsenal), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona), Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea)

The selection of Jobe Bellingham for the senior squad means he continues to follow in the footsteps of his older brother.

Both graduates of the Birmingham City academy, the brothers were regular selections in England youth line-ups.

Jobe joined Dortmund from Sunderland in summer 2025 in a deal worth up to Â£31m, having helped the Wearside club win promotion to the Premier League via the play-offs.

The move mirrored one made by Jude, 23, who played for the German side between 2020 and 2023 before signing for Real Madrid.

Tuchel said England Under-21 coach Lee Carsley had been "speaking very highly" of Jobe Bellingham "for a while".

"He is the captain of the under-21s so I think the door should always be open and the pathway should always be open for special performances over a long period of time and that is what Jobe has done," he added.

"He found his way and his rhythm with Dortmund, where he has had an excellent start to the season. He is a regular starter there and now very influential."

Bellingham has been preferred to Kobbie Mainoo, with Tuchel saying the Manchester United midfielder, who was an early withdrawal from the last squad, has had a "difficult spell with his club".

"The door is always open for younger players to overtake and make their mark," he added.

King has had a strong start to the Premier League season, scoring two goals and making one assist, and has played at every youth level for England.

The 19-year-old Fulham academy graduate has scored one goal in nine appearances for England Under-21s, and Tuchel called him "a fantastic character" who "gives us a bit of flexibility".

"We decided to nominate 22 outfield players for flexibility in training and he is the extra player in training, if you will," Tuchel added.

'Palmer misses too many opportunities to impress' - Tuchel

Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka misses out on the November fixtures after sustaining a quadriceps injury against Bayern Munich last month.

The Premier League champions believe the 25-year-old will be absent for six weeks after he was substituted early in the Champions League game against Bayern Munich.

Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott is also not selected after picking up an injury against Croatia in October.

The 23-year-old, who made his England debut in the first international break of the season and was described as "the complete package" by Tuchel, is reportedly in contention to return for the Cherries against Ipswich on Sunday.

Manchester United's Marcus Rashford and Newcastle's Tino Livramento, who both pulled out the last squad prior to any matches being played, also miss out with respective hip and knee injuries.

Como's Trevoh Chalobah is another absentee, while Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly and Rico Lewis have also not been selected.

James Garner of Everton and Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White retain their places after being added to England's last squad prior to any fixtures being played, while Arsenal's Ben White and Inter Milan's Djed Spence return for the first time since the summer.

The Arsenal pair of Declan Rice and Ezri Konsa, who both withdrew from the last England party, are fit and selected.

QOTSA leads the latest chart with Perfecth, their ninth studio album. It’s the seventh top 10 appearance for Josh Homme and Co., and their third leader after 2013’s …Like Clockwork and 2017’s Villains. Perfecth is the best seller on wax for the week, earning top spot on ARIA’s Vinyl Chart.

#738. A mysterious star system just 16 light-years away may be hiding habitable planets

A star system just 16 light-years from Earth has puzzled astronomers for more than 170 years. Now, researchers have uncovered a surprising explanation for a signal that once suggested a giant planet was hiding there. Although the discovery rules out certain massive planets, it also helps narrow the search for smaller worlds that could potentially support life.

Led by the University of Michigan, the new study examined 70 Ophiuchi AB, also known as 70 Oph AB, a nearby binary star system in which two stars orbit each other. Using an exceptionally sensitive analysis, scientists searched for planets as massive as Jupiter or larger. Instead of finding one, they determined that such planets do not exist within the regions they examined.

That result might initially seem disappointing, but it represents an important advance. The researchers achieved the most sensitive modern search for giant planets in this particular system, using an approach that was not intended to detect smaller worlds. The work, supported in part by NASA, therefore leaves open the possibility that other planets remain undiscovered.

Among those possibilities are planets the size of Saturn or smaller, including rocky worlds that might exist within the system's habitable zone. This is the region around a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to remain on a planet's surface, provided the planet has suitable atmospheric conditions. Because liquid water is essential to life as we know it, such worlds are especially interesting to astronomers searching for life beyond Earth.

The mystery surrounding 70 Oph AB began long before modern planet hunting. In 1855, British astronomer William Jacob proposed that the system contained a planet, making it the first star system to host an officially proposed exoplanet candidate. His claim was eventually rejected, but the possibility of undiscovered planets continued to intrigue astronomers for generations.

"It's a mix of disappointment and excitement," said Yiting Li, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We're finding out that there isn't a Jupiter-sized planet, but we're also opening the latest chapter on this historic system."

Unlike our solar system, which has only one star, roughly half of all stellar systems in the Milky Way contain at least two. These multiple star systems offer valuable opportunities to investigate how planets form, change over time, and potentially develop conditions suitable for life.

70 Oph AB is particularly attractive because of its proximity. Located approximately 16 light-years from Earth, it is the third closest binary star system to our planet, following Alpha Centauri (4.2 light-years) and 61 Cygni (11.4 light-years).

The new findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, also establish the orbits of the system's two stars, 70 Oph A and 70 Oph B, as some of the most precisely understood stellar orbits in the sky.

Future NASA Missions Could Search for Smaller Worlds

Knowing which planets are absent can be just as valuable as discovering new ones. By eliminating certain possibilities, the researchers have provided information that could make future searches more efficient and help astronomers focus on planets that remain within reach of upcoming observatories.

"The new limit enables us to design optimum search strategies in the future," said Michael Meyer, a senior co-author of the study and chair of the University of Michigan's astronomy department.

"In fact, the University of Michigan is part of a team studying a space mission called SHERA that will focus on binaries, where this system is one of a handful of targets. 70 Oph AB will certainly be a target of flagship missions, such as NASA's Habitable World Observatory."

Such missions could help scientists study smaller planets that current observations cannot yet detect or characterize. Rocky planets are especially important targets because they offer the possibility of environments similar to Earth, although finding one in a habitable zone would not by itself establish that life exists there.

Scientists Discover the True Source of a Mysterious Stellar Wobble

The research brought together scientists from more than a dozen institutions, including NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and IPAC at the California Institute of Technology.

Their analysis ruled out planets with masses equal to or greater than Jupiter's within specific parts of the system. Around 70 Oph A, no such planets were found within 5 astronomical units. Around 70 Oph B, they were excluded within half an astronomical unit. An astronomical unit is the average distance between Earth and the Sun, approximately 93 million miles.

These limits resolve a question that had persisted despite increasingly advanced observations. Although William Jacob's original claim from 1855 did not withstand later examination, measurements collected over the following 171 years had never completely eliminated the possibility of giant planets in the system's inner regions.

One particularly puzzling clue involved changes in the stars' radial velocity, which describes how quickly an object moves toward or away from Earth. Astronomers can use these changes to search for planets because an orbiting planet's gravity causes its host star to move slightly back and forth. This subtle motion produces a detectable "wobble" in measurements of the star's light.

For years, observations of 70 Oph AB revealed a wobble that could have been explained by a Jupiter-sized planet. The new research, however, points to a different cause.

To investigate, the team combined roughly a century of historical measurements with new observations from two major telescopes: the 6.5-meter Magellan Clay Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile and the 2.7-meter Harlan J. Smith Telescope at McDonald Observatory in Texas.

The resulting analysis was sensitive enough to distinguish the apparent planetary signal from changes occurring on the stars themselves. The researchers concluded that variations in stellar surface activity over time, rather than the gravitational influence of a giant planet, were responsible for the mysterious wobble.

"Yiting assembled an absolutely huge amount of data from all over the world and carefully explored all possibilities," Meyer said. "It's a cautionary tale about how stellar activity can mimic planet signals using the radial velocity."

The Search for Hidden Planets Is Far From Over

Despite ruling out giant planets in the surveyed regions, the findings do not mean 70 Oph AB is planet-free. Smaller planets could still orbit either star, and the system remains a promising destination for future observations.

The results illustrate an important challenge in the search for planets beyond our solar system. Stars are not perfectly stable objects, and changes in their activity can produce signals that resemble those created by orbiting planets. Separating these effects is essential for identifying genuine exoplanets, particularly smaller rocky worlds.

For 70 Oph AB, the latest discovery represents progress rather than a final answer. Scientists now have a clearer picture of what the system does not contain, along with better information for determining where to look next.

"The study sets an upper limit, not a ban, on planets," Li said. "Given how prevalent planets are in our universe and in the Milky Way, I would wager that we'll find there are other planets there."

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Heising-Simons Foundation.

On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet.

While it did end up flying by Mars, the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars.

When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars.

Ever since Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope to the red-tinted star and identified as a planet, Mars has captivated scientists' interests as to its nature. So it was of no surprise that as soon as we gained the ability to send missions into space, that the focus turned to the "fourth rock from the Sun."

As it turned out, though, reaching Mars, let alone entering its orbit or landing on its surface,, was and continues to be difficult.

Mars 1, despite its name, was actually the Soviet Union's fourth attempt at sending a probe to the planet. The first three ended in launch failures. Similar problems faced the United States, as well, but it was NASA's Mariner IV mission that became the first to successfully fly by Mars two years later.

Still, as humanity continues to push forward to the day people land on, explore and live on Mars, the 1962 Soviet mission stands as the first to get close to revealing the first details about the planet.

It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina.

That April 1 event — an incoming meteor, also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors.

Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic.

That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

This skyfall show is among a number of recent episodes that spotlight the value of combining multi-sensor data to not only portray fireball dynamics but also to help appreciate human-caused space debris impacts, as well as strengthening planetary defense knowhow.

Take, for instance, another extraterrestrial incident.

In this case, an April 24, 2025 fireball over south-central Alaska yielded one of the most densely recorded "seismoacoustic" datasets ever obtained for a nature-made bolide en route to busting up.

A network of 37 seismic stations, 16 single infrasound sensors, and four infrasound arrays recorded 30 ballistic and multiple fragmentation arrivals. All this was complemented by Doppler weather radar detections of falling meteorites and independent optical video observations.

Now, toss in for good measure yet another encounter.

A roughly 12-foot-wide (3.7 meters) space rock plowed through Earth's atmosphere over northwest Queensland, Australia, on May 20, 2023, accompanied by a raucous round of sonic booms. And U.S. government space-based sensors caught the fall.

Researchers later determined that the object underwent catastrophic fragmentation, producing one of the 20 most energetic events reported by NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS) since 1988 and the most energetic seen over Australia. It was equivalent to the explosion of a 7.1-kiloton bomb.

"For many fireballs, U.S. Government detections reported through NASA's CNEOS database provide an important starting point by establishing that an event occurred and, in many cases, providing basic parameters such as location, time and estimated energy," explained Elizabeth Silber, a senior research and development physicist at the U.S. Department of Energy's Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico.

"Civil and scientific observing systems can then add independent measurements that help refine and validate that initial characterization," said Silber.

CNEOS, which is based at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, is NASA's center for computing asteroid and comet orbits and their odds of striking Earth. CNEOS computes high-precision orbits for such objects in support of NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office.

"The Alaska event is an especially useful example, because it was not reported by U.S. Government sensors in the CNEOS database. In this case, the event was reconstructed almost entirely from civil and scientific observations," Silber told Space.com.

She said that the seismic and infrasound data constrained the trajectory and acoustic energy, the video provided independent optical information, and the weather radar detected material from the fireball falling to Earth.

"So, the real strength is that these systems provide different and complementary information," said Silber. "When a U.S. Government detection is available, civil data can independently validate it and add much more detail. When one is not available, as in this case [for Alaska], the civil networks can still provide a surprisingly complete reconstruction."

The Alaska study shows how valuable it is to put together diverse types of observations once an event has occurred, said Silber. Each measurement responds to a different part of the event.

"Seismic and infrasound sensors record the atmospheric shock waves and can constrain the trajectory, fragmentation and energy," she added. "Optical observations provide an independent view of the luminous flight. Doppler weather radar can detect surviving material after it has slowed and entered dark flight."

Bottom line: no single sensor tells you everything.

"Combining independent observations lets us move from simply knowing that an event occurred to determining how the object traveled through the atmosphere, where it fragmented, how much energy it released, and whether material may have survived to the ground," said Silber.

Researchers got pretty lucky with the April 1, 2026 event over the South Atlantic, according to NASA's Rob Landis, a planetary defense specialist: Two civilian spacecraft located at different locations in geosynchronous orbit allowed them to conduct a rather unique investigation of this bolide.

"With two civilian resources, we can actually discuss things more openly," Landis, who's now a visiting vehicle integration manager for the International Space Station at NASA's Johnson Space Center, told Space.com.

Lightning-watching instruments not designed for detecting bolides, he said, "afford the science community to discuss these events and these sensors in a forthright, open manner. These lightning imagers give us opportunistic bonus science for those who study the 'hard rain.'"

Landis said that, in his personal view, there's a lot of smaller stuff getting through the atmosphere.

"To the casual observer, these certainly produce wonderful natural fireworks and are mostly harmless," Landis said. But, he stressed, it's important to be able to distinguish between natural events and human-made ones.

"It would be a horrific tragedy if any nation responded to a natural event — if they misinterpret it as a preemptive strike," cautioned Landis.

So, in the big picture, having collaborative, multiple and independent ways to observe atmospheric entries is of benefit to planetary defense thinkers.

"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth," Silber said. "It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry — that is, how the object fragments, where it deposits its energy, how accurately we can reconstruct its trajectory and whether material survives to the ground."

Incoming events provide "real-world tests" of the methods and models used to answer those questions, said Silber.

Harkening back to the recent Alaska fireball fall, Silber said, was particularly valuable because it was unpredicted, yet the dense ground-based network allowed the trajectory and energetics to be reconstructed in considerable detail.

"From a planetary-defense perspective, that kind of redundancy is extremely useful. Space-based observations, seismic and infrasound networks, optical cameras, and weather radar each provide different information, and each has its own limitations," Silber said.

When several observation techniques are available, researchers can cross-check one another and produce a much more complete characterization of an event.

"That improves post-event situational awareness, helps validate physical models and strengthens our ability to interpret future atmospheric entries, whether they involve natural objects or artificial reentries," Silber concluded.

#735. Interscope Expands Into Brazil With Hip-Hop Artist BK, Supernova Entertainment Joint Venture

The new twin deals portend the label's significant expansion into the eighth-largest music market in the world, according to IFPI.

Interscope Records is branching out into Brazil, the company announced Friday (Nov. 6), unveiling two new deals in the country: the signing of hip-hop star BK, and a new joint venture/distribution deal with leading urban label Supernova Entertainment.

For BK, signing with Interscope coincides with the 10th anniversary of his debut album, Castelos & Ruinas; his first release for Interscope will be a remix of that album with new production and new collaborations. The new JV with Supernova encompasses the Brazilian urban label’s catalog and a partnership for new signings.

“We have shown through our successful track record over the past few years that wherever they come from, artists are attracted to the kind of global artist development platform we can provide at Interscope,” Interscope Capitol Miami executive vp/GM Jose Cedeño said in a statement. “Having BK as our first artist signing and Supernova as our first label deal, illustrate how serious our mission is to empower Brazilian artists to become global superstars.”

The Brazilian market has been a particular focus of the majors in recent years — one that reflects both investment in the country itself and the subsequent growth in subscription streaming and consumption in general. In March, IFPI reported that the Brazilian music market had grown by 14.1% year over year, much higher than the 6.4% growth of the industry overall, jumping over Canada to become the eighth-largest market in the world.

“Brazilian music and culture are having an extraordinary impact around the world right now,” Interscope Capitol chairman/CEO John Janick said in a statement. “We see an opportunity to leverage our legacy and current success in urban music for important Brazilian artists like BK and labels like Supernova Entertainment. We are excited to expand the resources and opportunities for Brazilian artists to move culture on a global level.”

Those opportunities were expanded upon by Victoria Oakley, IFPI’s CEO, in a new interview with Billboard this week. “I think we’re seeing the music economy emerge at the same time as we’re seeing the Brazilian economy emerge,” Oakley said. “It’s also a place of phenomenal talent, and their export story is much more successful so far, principally across their own region. But I think given that most of the music is in Portuguese and not in Spanish, so the obvious sellable market isn’t there in quite the same way, they’ve done a phenomenal job with their export story and they are on the increase. They too have a government that I think, from early on, places culture as an important part of the education system, and I think that is quite an important first step that we often don’t see the benefits of until much later.”

“BK’s authenticity and distinctly Brazilian voice have made him one of the defining figures in Brazilian hip-hop,” Interscope’s urban music co-presidents Laura Carter and Ramon Alvarez-Smikle said in a statement. “His music reflects the depth, originality and cultural influence of hip-hop both in Brazil and globally. Our partnership with Supernova continues Interscope’s tradition of working with visionary labels that are deeply connected to their artists and culture, and we’re excited to deepen our commitment to hip-hop in Brazil together.”

#734. What the rift within the Tsikhanouski family means for the Belarusian opposition in exile

Siarhei Tsikhanouski criticizes the work of his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and her office. He also questions her legitimacy. What are the implications for Belarusian political forces in exile?

Blogger and dissident Siarhei Tsikhanouski , 48, was detained in Belarus in May 2020, after he had announced to challenge the country's ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, in the upcoming presidential elections. In December 2021, Tsikhanouski was convicted to 18 years in prison, in part for organizing "mass unrest."

After his arrest his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, took his place and challenged Lukashenko as presidential candidate. Despite allegations of large-scale vote-rigging, Lukashenko was declared the winner of the election in August 2020. This triggered unprecedented mass protests across the country. They were violently suppressed, and thousands of government critics were arrested or fled into exile. Tsikhanouskaya also fled her homeland and became the leading representative of the Belarusian democratic movement.

In June 2025, Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released after nearly five years in prison and was forcibly taken out of the country.

Some 14 months after his release, the blogger has re-activated his YouTube channel, where he not only denounces Alexander Lukashenko's regime, but also Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's office, Belarusian media in exile, political analysts and others. Thousands of people follow his streams.

In one of them, Tsikhanouski claims that while Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya obviously enjoyed "a certain legitimacy from the European Union," the people who were living "quietly and silently" in Belarus today had not granted her any. He said that many of those who had voted for her as joint candidate of Belarus' opposition were regretting this today.

Tsikhanouski has suggested that a supervisory board should be established under the label "United Office of Demoratic Forces." It would be made up of "former presidential candidates, protest leaders and iconic figures of the revolution," including himself and his wife. "There would not be a full legitimacy but one which was at least granted by Belarusians," Tsikhanouski said, adding that such a supervisory board could oversee the distribution of grant funds.

Speaking about his wife, he said: "Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya was a so-called technical candidate, who received the votes of all those who were against Lukashenko. The percentage of votes she received in the 2020 election was negligible because no one knew who she was. She was allowed to run because she did not pose a threat for the regime, and because she had neither supporters nor political experience."

Asked by DW what his goals were, Siarhei  Tsikhanouski refused to comment and referred to his livestreams instead. The former political prisoner is residing in the US and is, by his own account, currently unemployed. At the beginning of summer he said he was living in Los Angeles, learning English, preparing for university studies and writing a book. It is also known that his children — a teenage son and a younger daughter — temporarily stayed with him in the US. Today, however, they attend school in Poland, where Tsikhanouskaya resides.

Neither she nor her office have commented on the family situation or her husband's allegations. Even before the public dispute, the leader of the Belarusian democratic forces avoided commenting on her husband. Asked about his activities, she often suggested to approach him directly.

Speaking to DW in December 2025, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya merely said: "What happens in the public sphere and what happens at home, are different things. I understand Siarhei's deep traumatization and also his very strong reactions to certain events. Siarhei was in prison for five years, and I look at it with great understanding. This is why I'm not going public or making any comments. We'll deal with it among ourselves."

During the 32-year-long rule of the Lukashenko regime, the Belarusian opposition has weathered many crises and conflicts. Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's leadership role has been called into question more than once. However, she and her team have always managed to work themselves out of difficult situations during the last couple of years. But will she still be able to do that now, with her own husband having turned into her critic?

Siarhei Tsikhanouski had gone back to his own self, said political scientist Yury Drakakhrust: "With all his idiosyncrasies, his style of debate, which is not exactly in line with common practice. This is likely to strike many as odd, including Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's international partners."

Tsikhanouski, Drakakhrust pointed out, insisted that he was the key figure of the 2020 events, which is why he was entitled to all the benefits, privileges, recognition and invitations. But there was no way back.

"Even if we assume that Tsikhanouski is right, that he was the central figure, what good would it do today?" he asked. "If, suddenly, hundreds of thousands of Belarusians watched his livestreams, collected funds, formed local groups or associations in Tsikhanouski's name, then perhaps it would be possible to turn back the wheel. But this will hardly be the case."

Drakakhrust described the current situation within the democratic forces as a "crisis." He doubted that Tsikhanouski would be able to reach an agreement with all the members of the supervisory board he has proposed. Furthermore, his wife, in particular, had since established certain assets, resources, and a status for herself through her office.

"Tsikhanouskaya is being received at high levels, if not as an elected president, then as a leader for Belarus and Belarusian democracy. She's not regarded as just one of several democratic leaders from Belarus," the political scientist said.

He pointed out that not only Tsikhanouskaya, but also other actors from the 2020 election campaign are in exile. They, however, had not achieved a similar level of representation or comparable access to resources. "She has surpassed them as a politician, and that's what counts."

Drakakhrust said that the Belarusian government views disputes among the opposition with a touch of irony, occasionally adding fuel to the fire: "Basically, they don't care who wins. The main thing is that there is conflict, bickering and mutual vilification."

#733. 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history

Deep within an ice cap in northwestern Tibet, scientists have uncovered evidence of a remarkable frozen record that may stretch back more than 128,000 years. The discovery suggests that ice high in the mountains has survived since the last ice age and could provide an extraordinary window into Earth's ancient climate.

The findings extend the known glacial record from the region by more than 100,000 years, making these the oldest ice cores ever recovered from this part of Tibet. They also offer rare evidence of how mountain glaciers endured major changes in Earth's climate.

Researchers reached their conclusions by examining ice cores collected from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015. Despite being drilled 23 years apart, the samples revealed strikingly similar patterns of oxygen isotopes, which scientists use to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The close match indicates that the ice has preserved a reliable and reproducible record of climate history.

"Reproducibility of the records within a given ice cap is extremely important," said Lonnie Thompson, lead author of the study, professor of earth sciences and senior research scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center at The Ohio State University. "If you get an identical record a quarter of a century later, it can tell you a lot about the behavior of the ice over time."

How Scientists Dated the Ancient Tibetan Ice

Determining the age of ice that has remained frozen for tens of thousands of years is no simple task. To establish a more accurate timeline, the international research team turned to advanced dating methods involving radioactive isotopes of beryllium and chlorine.

These naturally occurring radioactive forms of elements decay at predictable rates, making them valuable tools for identifying events deep in Earth's environmental history. In this case, researchers used them to detect evidence of the Leschamp Geomagnetic Excursion, a dramatic disturbance in Earth's magnetic field that occurred more than 41,000 years ago and left distinctive chemical signatures in the ice.

The team then compared its findings with oxygen isotope records preserved in nearby Tibetan cave deposits. Together, the evidence suggests that the Guliya ice record may extend well beyond 128,000 years into the past.

"It's a really critical finding, because outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that go back that far," he said. "Records out of Huascarán only go back over 30,000 years, not over 100,000, so that makes Guliya a very unique record."

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

A Frozen Climate Record From the Last Ice Age

Ice cores are among scientists' most valuable sources of information about ancient climates. As snow accumulates and gradually becomes compressed into ice, it can preserve chemical clues about the atmosphere and environmental conditions at the time. By examining different layers, researchers can piece together how climate changed over thousands of years.

However, interpreting these records depends on knowing when each layer formed. Without a reliable timeline, even an exceptionally well-preserved ice core can be difficult to understand.

That uncertainty had complicated earlier interpretations of the Guliya ice cap. Previous research suggested that its record reached back only to the middle of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began nearly 12,000 years ago following the last ice age.

The new evidence establishes that at least some of the ice is considerably older than the Holocene. This also has important implications for understanding whether large ice masses in Tibet persisted as the planet emerged from the last glacial period.

"If we only had Holocene-era ice in Tibet, that would mean that the big ice sheets from the last ice age didn't persist through the early Holocene," said Thompson. "But evidence shows that it did."

What the Discovery Reveals About Earth's Glacial History

The Guliya ice cap's unusual geography may help explain why it has preserved such an exceptionally old climate record. Its high elevation and surrounding terrain likely contributed to conditions that allowed ancient ice to remain in place through major environmental changes.

Beyond establishing the ice's age, researchers hope that a more precise timeline will help answer fundamental questions about the history of Earth's glaciers. Knowing when major periods of glaciation began, how long they lasted, and when the ice retreated is essential for reconstructing the planet's natural climate cycles.

"When did ice start forming on the planet and what did those natural processes of loss look like?" said Thompson. "We need to know those things, and the only way you can really demonstrate it is with accurate time scales on these records."

The revised timeline also creates new opportunities to investigate the Guliya ice cores in greater detail. Researchers plan to study additional samples to determine how other indicators of past climate and environmental conditions fit into this much longer history.

Those future analyses could reveal information that was previously overlooked or interpreted differently because scientists did not fully understand the age of the ice.

For Thompson, one of the most encouraging aspects of the discovery is how consistently the different measurements support the same interpretation.

"The big picture is that our results tell a very consistent story," he said. "If you get the science right, it's consistent. It's our understanding of what it's trying to tell us that has to catch up."

The research received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. Ohio State co-authors include Mary Davis and Ellen Mosley-Thompson. Other contributors were Juerg Beer of the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology; Christof Vockenhuber and Marcus Christl of ETH Zurich in Switzerland; Tandong Yao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences; and Ninglian Wang and Ling Fang of Northwest University in China.

Nintendo's sci-fi shooter franchise is in dire straits, but we've got the solution to Samus's problems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Metroid Prime 4: Beyond was, unfortunately, not the return many were hoping for when it finally arrived on Nintendo Switch consoles in 2025. After five years in development at Retro Studios, the original makers of the Metroid Prime series, fans were greeted with annoying side characters, a bike for Samus to roam the barren landscape on, and a deeply unsatisfying ending.

It’s a shame, considering how beloved the Metroid Prime series has been since the first title’s 2002 debut for the Nintendo GameCube. Many franchises were jumping from 2D to 3D at the turn of the millennium, and there were plenty of failures — but Metroid wasn’t one of them. The two sequels would enhance how players control Samus with powerful weapons and a multiplayer mode, but the 18-year gap between Metroid Prime 3 and 4 left players expecting something special.

Metroid Prime 4: Beyond’s average reception left fans wondering where the series can go next. It’s admittedly strange that Metroid Prime 2 and 3 have yet to debut on Nintendo Switch, either through the Nintendo Online service or as remasters.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has just dropped for Switch 2, and seeing Nintendo leverage one of the best games of all time for a modern take has given us an idea: let's give the Metroid Prime trilogy the remake treatment, taking inspiration from Capcom’s efforts with Resident Evil.

From 2002’s Resident Evil remake to the more recent successes with Resident Evil 2 & 4, Capcom has managed to recreate the feeling and survival horror tropes of the originals while modernizing the gameplay.

Whether it's the constant tension of being stalked by a Terminator-like Mr. X in 2019’s Resident Evil 2, or the palpable paranoia you feel exploring in Resident Evil 4 — the skin might be new, but the bones are undeniably "Resi."

Even recently-announced Resident Evil: Veronica — whilst a remake of 1999’s Code: Veronica — looks set to be a brand new take that evokes the feeling of the original game, but brings it into the modern era.

Prime 4 felt like a game out of time. Sure, it looked the part, but it felt decidedly like a GameCube game. So why not take a leaf out of Capcom's book, apply their "recapturing the vibes" mindset for a Metroid Prime Trilogy Remake, using the Prime 4 engine as its foundation.

2023’s Metroid Prime Remastered showed off the venerable title with better textures and widescreen support, but a remake powered by the fourth game’s engine could showcase the opening and Tallon IV in a whole new light.

Similar to 2002’s Resident Evil Remake with the Spencer Mansion, places would feel familiar but fresh, thanks to updated graphics, better sound, and support for HD Rumble 2 that could help the player become more immersed in the game. And of course, you can change a few things to play off people's expectations.

If Nintendo is feeling brave, the reimagining could even begin at the end of Zero Mission, which is set just before Metroid Prime. Controlling Samus with all her abilities, facing off against Mother Brain in an area not seen in 3D, could be a great introduction to old and new players, as well as giving the opportunity to remake an area from a previous title. Then, players could escape to Samus’ ship, with the ability to pilot it to the Orpheron ship, where Prime begins.

A remake (or remakes) would obviously mean a big step-up in graphics and gameplay across all three games, but it could also herald the long-awaited return of its multiplayer mode from Metroid Prime 2, something that Metroid Prime 4: Beyond bizarrely left out.

Up to four players could take part in one of two modes here - Deathmatch and Bounty Mode, which had players compete against one another by collecting coins to win matches. There were four arenas to choose from, with an additional two to unlock when players got far enough in Prime 2’s single-player mode.

It was a fun time, and its absence in Prime 4: Beyond felt like a big miss, especially with the prospect of playing this mode online with others and using the Switch 2 features like Game Chat.

A remake could fix this injustice, and even expand on the concept by offering new multiplayer modes alongside maps based on locations from across the Prime series. You could even add a co-op mode for the campaign, and a horde mode for co-op fans to enjoy online too.

As it stands in 2026, the Metroid series feels adrift once more. Metroid Prime 4: Beyond will be lost to the sands of time, a mediocre entry in a series filled with bangers. As the latest Nintendo Direct eagerly showcased Donkey Kong, Zelda, and plenty of third-party releases, Samus was notably absent. Sure, she's just had a game, but it's hard not to be nervous after the drought that Metroid players had to suffer in the 2010s.

Capcom was in a similar lull after 2012’s disappointing Resident Evil 6, a bloated and confusing entry that made players fear the end of the series. But the seventh entry, alongside the Resident Evil 2 Remake in 2019, breathed new life into the franchise, which has proved as tough to kill as any of Umbrella's bioweapons.

Metroid's fate feels equally in the balance right now, and in a world where game studios are closing down and rivals like Microsoft are shrinking their focus to big-hitter franchises, Nintendo could easily let Metroid fall back into obscurity. Refocusing on what makes the series iconic is the key to its success, and modern remakes of the originals might just be what they need to rediscover that Metroid magic.

There are some easy wins out there to keep fans engaged; it’d still be great to see more games appear on the Nintendo Online service, like Metroid Prime 2, and we'd love more 2D entries after the excellent Metroid Dread, but nothing hits like Prime, and Prime isn't hitting right now.

If not, then I fear Samus will be riding her Vi-O-La into the sunset, deep within the barren wasteland of Sol Valley for the foreseeable future.

Daryl is an entertainment writer and author of two books—The Making of Tomb Raider and 50 Years of Boss Fights.

#731. Stevie Nicks Predicted the Midterm Blue Wave in a Moving Poem: ‘The Light Creates a Circle of Angels’

The Fleetwood Mac singer said she wrote "Morning Symphony" three weeks before Tuesday's massive rebuke of the Trump agenda.

While many Americans watched Tuesday’s midterm election results with either great anticipation or resigned dread, Stevie Nicks was not sweating the final tally at all because she already knew how the night would end.

The Fleetwood Mac singer and solo star revealed in a post on X that she wrote a poem on Oct. 18 as a kind of wish into the universe. “It was sort of like a little prayer for the coming elections,” she said. “I really believed that what has happened was going to happen; it just had to. Good almost wins … I didn’t have time to get it out before the election — so here it is. That’s the dream …”

The dream came true, as Nicks — who endorsed former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election — and the rest of the nation watched the electorate soundly rebuke the second Trump term agenda by giving Democrats a historic blue wave victory that has swept them into the majority in both the House and Senate, in addition to flipping five governorships and racking up massive wins on the local, state and national level.

In the poem titled “Morning Symphony,” Nicks muses on the beauty of early mornings and her dog Lily, her sadness about what is going on in the country, ending with a final, flickering hope that the light will win out over darkness.

I get up and walk to the window and I don’t sleep —

Back in August, Nicks, 78, made a surprise appearance at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival where they performed the Fleetwood Mac classic “Landslide.” The two women also contributed to the soundtrack of Practical Magic 2, which featured “Landslide” and Rodrigo’s “The Cure.”

#730. NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s

NASA's Juno spacecraft has uncovered remarkable new details about how Jupiter withstands the constant stream of high-energy particles flowing from the Sun. The findings reveal that the solar system's largest planet relies on a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth does.

Led by scientists at the University of Iowa, the research provides the most detailed observations yet of Jupiter's bow shock, an invisible boundary where particles from the Sun encounter the planet's magnetic environment. The discovery reveals important differences in how Jupiter and Earth respond to these incoming particles.

Beyond Jupiter, the results could also help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.

How Jupiter Protects Itself From the Solar Wind

The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. These particles travel through space at tremendous speeds, often faster than the speed at which sound waves move through the surrounding plasma. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it encounters a boundary known as the bow shock.

At Earth, this boundary plays an important protective role. It slows and heats the incoming particles, helping redirect much of the solar wind around the planet. Without this process, more harmful particles could reach Earth's atmosphere, potentially making conditions less favorable for life.

Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field, and gaseous composition make it a particularly interesting place to study how these boundaries behave. Scientists have long wanted to understand whether Jupiter handles the solar wind differently from Earth and what those differences might reveal about other objects throughout the universe.

Scientists Discover a More Complex Defense System

Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as "harmonics," create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth.

The process can be compared to music. Just as several notes played together produce a richer sound than a single note, plasma waves containing multiple frequencies can interact with incoming particles in more complex ways. This allows Jupiter's bow shock to transfer energy to more particles, heating them and reducing their speed.

Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses plasma waves concentrated around a single frequency. That simpler arrangement is generally sufficient for the conditions encountered near our planet.

"Jupiter has found its own way to deal with the solar wind, through plasma waves that are stronger and exhibit richer harmonic structures," says Jayasri Joseph, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa and the study's corresponding author. "That's important because if you have multiple frequencies, you can heat more particles in the solar wind and slow them down."

The researchers identified another striking difference in how the two planets interact with the solar wind.

Before incoming particles reach Jupiter's main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets. These additional regions help slow the solar wind before it arrives at the primary shock boundary.

Earth's bow shock, in contrast, generally serves as the main region where the incoming solar wind is slowed and redirected. Jupiter's additional shock structures reveal a more complicated process for managing the energy carried by solar particles.

"Earth does not need to take these extra steps to handle the solar wind because the impact isn't as powerful," says Bill Kurth, a research scientist in Iowa's Department of Physics and Astronomy and a coauthor of the study.

Kurth has participated in NASA's Juno mission since the spacecraft launched in 2011.

What Jupiter Can Teach Us About Exploding Stars

Although these observations focus on Jupiter, their significance could extend far beyond our solar system.

Shock waves occur throughout the universe, particularly in environments where enormous amounts of energy are released. Some of the most extreme examples are found in supernova remnants, the expanding clouds of material left behind when certain dying stars explode.

These cosmic shock waves are vastly more powerful than those encountered near Jupiter. However, the physical processes that control how energy moves through plasma share important similarities. By examining Jupiter's bow shock in unprecedented detail, scientists can investigate mechanisms that would be much harder to measure directly around distant stars.

"Because even more powerful shocks occur around astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, Jupiter's bow shock offers a nearby natural laboratory for exploring and for understanding how nature converts enormous amounts of flow energy into heat and energetic particles," Joseph says.

Understanding these processes could improve scientific models of how shock waves transfer energy, heat particles, and shape environments across the universe.

NASA's Juno Makes Unprecedented Measurements

The breakthrough was made possible by observations Juno collected in December 2024. The NASA spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter since July 2016, providing researchers with an extraordinary opportunity to investigate the giant planet and its surrounding environment.

A key part of the discovery came from the Juno Waves instrument, which was designed and built by physicists at the University of Iowa. The instrument measures electric and magnetic wave activity, allowing scientists to study the behavior of plasma around Jupiter.

Earlier spacecraft had detected the presence of bow shocks at outer planets, but they lacked the measurements needed to reveal the detailed structure of the plasma waves involved. Juno's observations have now provided a much clearer picture of how these waves behave at Jupiter.

The findings were published online on July 31 in Nature Communications in a study titled "Plasma wave observations from Juno spacecraft at the Jovian bow shock."

Additional contributors from the University of Iowa included Allison Jaynes, an associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, along with Jeremy Faden and Chris Piker, who provide research support in the same department.

The international research team also included Lynn Wilson III of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; John Connerney of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and the Space Research Corporation; Frederic Allegrini of the Southwest Research Institute and the University of Texas-San Antonio; Rob Wilson of the University of Colorado-Boulder; Ali Sulaiman of the University of Minnesota; Scott Boltion and Robert Ebert of the Southwest Research Institute; and Barry Mauk of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.

Materials provided by University of Iowa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Liftoff occurred today (Nov. 2) at 11:41 a.m. ET.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rocket Lab launched its 99th mission to date today (Nov. 2), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite toward orbit.

An Electron rocket lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site today at 11:41 a.m. EST (1641 GMT; 5:41 a.m. on Nov. 3 local New Zealand time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Sea God Surveys," is carrying an Earth-observing radar satellite to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Japanese company iQPS. All went according to plan: The spacecraft was deployed at an altitude of 357 miles (575 kilometers), Rocket Lab announced about 56 minutes after launch.

"The Sea God Surveys" was Rocket Lab's 10th launch to date for iQPS, which is assembling a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO.

SAR satellites offer advantages over those that view our planet in optical wavelengths. They can peer through cloud cover, for example, and study our planet at night as well as during the day.

Today's launch was the 99th overall for Rocket Lab and the 90th for the two-stage, 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron, which gives small satellites dedicated rides to space. The workhorse vehicle has now flown 17 times this year.

Rocket Lab's other nine launches to date have been conducted by HASTE, a suborbital version of Electron that allows customers to test their tech in the hypersonic flight environment. HASTE (short for "Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron") debuted in June 2023 and generally flies classified payloads.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:55 a.m. ET on Nov. 2 with news of successful launch, then again at 1 p.m. EST with news of successful satellite deployment.
